statements.text: So when you look at the utilization of AI you should be able to push forward with problem-solving in the absence of individuals, by having the brainpower that is there to distill what you are hearing.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI applications to cyber operations, featuring testimony from expert witnesses including Dr. Eric Horvitz.

statements.text: Can you commit, as you've done with consumer data, not to train ChatGPT, OpenAI Jukebox, or other AI models on artists and songwriters' copyrighted works or use their voices and their likenesses without first receiving their consent?
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI oversight where Senator Blackburn presses an OpenAI executive on copyright and consent.

statements.text: Well, Senator Durbin just said, you know, and I think it's a fair warning to you all, if we're not involved in this from the get-go, and you all already are a long way down the path on this, but if we don't step in, then this gets away from you. So, are you working with the copyright office? Are you considering protections for content generators and creators in generative AI?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing on AI rules, questioning industry witnesses.

statements.text: But I think, as we have talked with them, Mr. Chairman, one of the things that continues to come up is, yes, Professor Marcus, as you were saying, the EU, different entities, are ahead of us in this, but we have never established a federally given preemption for online privacy, for data security, and put some of those foundational elements in place, which is something that we need to do as we look at this. And it will require that Commerce Committee, Judiciary Committee decide how we move forward so that people own their virtual you.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, Senator Blackburn questioning witnesses including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

statements.text: And there's the potential for the pattern recognition capabilities of AI models to be a countermeasure against the production of counterfeit, inauthentic content such as what terrorized Ms. DeStefano. [...] Which capability is advancing more rapidly? The ability to detect what is fake or the ability to produce it?
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Human Rights hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: And do you know of any American companies that were involved in creating or funding AI tech that was used to surveil citizens in China?
statements.context: Senate hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, featuring a question from Senator Blackburn to a witness named Mr. Cain.

statements.text: It seems as though a company that releases a tool that can clone a person's voice should be able to predict some of the ways the tool would be misused. And if they don't put sufficient safety measures in place, they should be held legally accountable.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Human Rights hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, June 13, 2023.

statements.text: we need to make a conscious effort to consider the potential impact that those technologies could have on human rights and on how we approach issues such as data collection, data retention, surveillance, and, of course, deepfakes.
statements.context: Opening statement at a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Human Rights hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights.

statements.text: We fielded several firsthand accounts of how this technology can be weaponized against human beings in our homes and on a national scale.
statements.context: Senate floor remarks by Senator Marsha Blackburn summarizing a Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and human rights.

statements.text: And you also mentioned the right of publicity laws, and of course, those are State level laws. [...] we don't have a federally preemptive right to publicity law.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI and copyright, Part II.

statements.text: We know that to create artistic works, AI systems must train on data scraped from existing artistic works. If you look at how this technology has advanced, it becomes clear that generative AI is often trained on popular music that was used without the copyright holder's permission. One AI model that we reviewed was trained on a staggering 280,000 hours of music. There is not a reasonable person who would ever suggest that the writers and artists were compensated fairly for that 280,000 hours of use of their products that was used to train AI to mimic and clone their voices and their words.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Marsha Blackburn during an Artificial Intelligence executive session, surveying AI's impact on Tennessee industries and urging congressional guardrails.

statements.text: Superhuman AI. Superhuman AI. I think all of you agree we're not decades away. We're perhaps just a couple of years away.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI regulation, during the second round of questions led by Chair Blumenthal following Senator Blackburn's remarks.

statements.text: Right. So, you would say existing law is not sufficient for AI? [...] Correct.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI regulation principles, featuring an exchange between Senator Blackburn and Professor Russell.

statements.text: And then you look at the entertainment industry and the voice cloning, and you look at what our entertainers, our songwriters, our artists, our authors, our publishers, our TV actors, our TV producers are facing with AI, and to them, it is an absolute way that they're robbing them of their ability to make a living off of their creative work.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI regulation principles, where Senator Blackburn questions a witness about protecting creative-industry workers from AI-generated imitations.

statements.text: I think there needs to be absolutely a requirement to disclose if the system is harvesting the data from individual conversations.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI regulation oversight, where Senator Blackburn questions witnesses about consumer privacy protections for AI.

statements.text: This swift rate of advancement, however, has caused many concerns. Many of the discussions that I have heard around AI has focused on the doomsday scenarios. While it is important to prevent catastrophic events, we must also not lose sight of the transformational benefits of AI. [...] That is why any regulatory action from Congress, or from Federal agencies, must balance safety with the preservation of an innovative economy.
statements.context: Opening statement at a Senate hearing on AI transparency.

statements.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Espinel, I want to come to you first. Because I know that the EU is looking at implementing their AI Act later this year. I was recently over there, and working on the privacy issue, and holding some meetings, and I think they are a little bit frustrated that we haven't moved forward on some of these guidelines and governance that would help our innovators here in the country. So talk for just a minute about how your members would navigate a patchwork system around the globe when it comes to AI and the guardrails that are going to be put around it?
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI transparency where a senator questions an industry witness about navigating divergent international AI regulations.

statements.text: But we are looking at some of the reports on surveillance with the CCP surveilling the Uyghurs, with Iran surveilling women. [...] prohibition of biometric surveillance in public spaces, prohibition of emotion recognition.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight, during a Q&A exchange between Senator Blackburn and Professor Hartzog.

statements.text: And I want to thank my colleagues, Senators Klobuchar, and Hawley, Coons, and Collins for taking a first step toward addressing the harms that may result from deepfakes, impersonation, all of the potential perils that we've identified here. [...] And then banning the deepfakes and impersonations is another approach.
statements.context: Senator Blackburn questioning witnesses at a Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI legislation.

statements.text: It is vital that we develop an understanding of what it is going to take to put the guardrails in place for AI. We are going to need to continue regular discussions between policymakers and the industry. [...] But we must stay focused and remember that AI raises the same concerns that plague other technological innovations. [...] U.S. regulations must not hurt the ability of U.S. companies to dominate, but the lack of any governing standards can be just as damaging.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Sen. Marsha Blackburn following an AI forum hosted by the Majority Leader, discussing AI regulation, data privacy, and national security concerns.

statements.text: What we are concerned about is restrictions on the ways in which companies handle consumer data or looking at bias in the algorithms used to fuel AI applications. So, would you confirm—would you support the FTC going beyond the authority that they have been given when it comes to AI?
statements.context: Senate confirmation hearing for nominees to the FTC and CPSC, where Senator Blackburn questions an FTC nominee about the scope of the agency's AI authority.

statements.text: we are all very concerned about continuing to bolster our leadership, whether it is going to deal with semiconductors, broadband, AI, quantum, the microelectronics that we were just discussing. [...] we have got to make certain that the CCP-controlled entities don't benefit as we move forward implementing CHIPS.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee oversight hearing on Chips and Science Act implementation, featuring questions to officials about technology competition with China.

statements.text: And the danger to their livelihoods is real because they are not being compensated for their music that is used to train AI models that are actually going to take away the ability for them to make money on what they have created. [...] AI is going to mimic them and use name, image, likeness, voice cloning and take away more of their ability.
statements.context: Senate floor speech during National Country Music Month executive session, advocating for music-industry legislation including the American Music Fairness Act, the HITS Act, and the NO FAKES Act.

statements.text: Now we're seeing bias against conservatives in some of the AI tools and training, and there are a couple of examples that we really need to put on the record.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI oversight focused on the future of journalism, where Senator Blackburn raised concerns about political bias in AI tools.

statements.text: I think that if we try to get to a point of legislating fake versus not fake, true versus false, we end up in a very dangerous teritory, and similarly around bias. What all of these models do is reflect the biases of society. I'll take you, as you say, that media are generally liberal, and thus what they ingest is going to be that way.
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI oversight focused on the future of journalism, where Senator Blackburn questions a witness about bias in AI models.

statements.text: you've said that you agree with OpenAI's models using materials, training AI models on publicly available material.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI oversight and the future of journalism, featuring testimony from Professor Jeff Jarvis.

statements.text: There are deficiencies, there are discrepancies. You have coding that calls for this, this, and this, and then over here you have this new technology. So this came up at the roundtable. So, talk to me a little bit—let us drill down a bit more on these deficiencies and these gaps, and how can CMS move forward and fix that, so that patients have the access to the best possible— [...]
statements.context: Senate hearing on AI in healthcare, Senator Blackburn questioning a witness about CMS reimbursement gaps.

statements.text: And we can't afford to get AI wrong.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the No Fakes Act regarding unauthorized digital replicas.

statements.text: we've heard—some commentators are talking about, well, you've got existing law, when it comes to privacy or to personal property and intellectual property protections, and so you can rest on that existing law [...] Talk to me about why that is not sufficient.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the No Fakes Act regarding protection from unauthorized digital replicas.

statements.text: I'm deeply concerned about what is happening to the creative community and working on NO FAKES and making certain that there is a way for artists to protect that name, image, likeness, their voice—that there is a way for them to exercise their constitutional right to protect their intellectual property and to benefit from that property.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the No Fakes Act, which would protect individuals from unauthorized AI-generated digital replicas.

statements.text: This threat is especially magnified as China seeks to become the world leader in artificial intelligence by the time we get to 2030. China plans for AI to power its vast surveillance state, and data collection and retention is at the heart of their strategy.
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee hearing on data security and consumer protection, chaired by Senator Cantwell.

statements.text: And as Senator Rosen just said, it is so vitally important to know who owns the virtual you—who has that and what are they doing with it and now as we are looking at AI I think Federal privacy legislation is more important than ever because you have got to put that foundational legislation in place in order to be able to legislate to a privacy standard [...]
statements.context: Senate Commerce Committee hearing on AI and privacy, Senator Blackburn opening remarks before questioning witnesses.

statements.text: So when you look at advancements and changes in AI five years down the road what do you expect? Ten years down the road what do you expect?
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'Protecting Consumers from Artificial Intelligence Enabled Fraud and Scams,' where Senator Blackburn questions expert witness Mr. Farid.

statements.text: Now, the fraudsters that are utilizing AI to deceive consumers are—have gotten crafty when it comes to creating these highly personalized and convincing attacks and I think what is surprising to a lot of people is the fact that they are doing this at scale, and the replication of these attacks and the tailored e-mails, the text messages, the images—as the Chairman showed the altered images—and those are used to trick people to click that link, and then once they have clicked that link they are then downloading malware. [...] And we know that it is also going to require that we move forward with having an actual online privacy standard, which we have never passed.
statements.context: Opening statement at a Senate hearing on protecting consumers from AI-enabled fraud and scams.

statements.text: S. 1269. A bill to promote United States leadership in technical standards by directing the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the Department of State to take certain actions to encourage and enable United States participation in developing standards and specifications for artificial intelligence and other critical and emerging technologies [...] to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
statements.context: Introduction of bills and joint resolutions on the Senate floor, recorded in the Congressional Record.

statements.text: On Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, AI chatbots have engaged in romantic fantasies with underage users, even carrying on explicit discussions of sexual acts with children. They know this is happening.
statements.context: Senate floor introductory statement by Sen. Marsha Blackburn on the reintroduction of the Kids Online Safety Act (S. 1748).

statements.text: There are all of these pieces of legislation dealing with AI that we haven't passed.
statements.context: Senate floor speech during a legislative session, urging colleagues to strike a provision (section 40012) from a bill.

statements.text: How are you going to approach firewalling copyrighted content in training of these LLMs and then allowing current event or conversation? [...] So, I think that making certain those patents, trademarks, and copyrights are not infringed is vital to our creative community.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'AI've Got a Plan: America's AI Action Plan,' where Senator Blackburn questions a witness about intellectual property protections in AI model training.

statements.text: Senator Warner and I have a standard setting bill that you all may want to incorporate in what you are doing. We are quite concerned about the U.S. retaining the ability to set standards.
statements.context: Senate hearing titled 'AI've Got a Plan: America's AI Action Plan' where Senator Blackburn raises AI standards legislation.

statements.text: And Senator Blumenthal talked earlier, as you all know, we have worked for years on the Kids Online Safety Act that would give that toolbox, that would put requirements on social media and on these platforms, and would require there to be a responsibility, a safety by design, and a duty of care so that you can hold a social media platform to account.
statements.context: Senate hearing examining harms to children from AI chatbots and social media platforms.

statements.text: OK. Thank you because I am going to put some things up that Gemma did. [...] Gemma created an entire falsehood around Mr. Starbuck saying he had been accused of child rape—totally false, totally false. [...] It made up articles.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing investigating government jawboning of Big Tech, where Senator Blackburn confronted a tech witness about biased LLM outputs.

statements.text: The American public deserves to know that, with these AI models, the information is going to be accurate. It is going to be transparent. It is going to be fair, and it is not going to be a tool that is going to be used to fabricate and to smear conservatives.
statements.context: Senate floor speech by Senator Marsha Blackburn during a government funding debate, pivoting to AI after discussing healthcare subsidies.

statements.text: Especially with AI, bad actors are only getting faster, smarter, and harder to stop. [...] Live Nation and Ticketmaster have repeatedly called on Congress and regulators to act in this space by enhancing legislative and regulatory protections.
statements.context: Written response from Live Nation/Ticketmaster submitted for the record at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the live entertainment industry.

statements.text: Scalpers are using AI-powered bots and software programs to scoop up hundreds and thousands of tickets at a time.
statements.context: Senate floor remarks by Senator Blackburn on winter storm recovery and online ticket-scalping practices.
